blocks.text: But the Arabs teach us much more about the bird قارية [qāriya] karia, which Damir describes thus: القارية كسارية طاير قصير الرجلين طويل المنقار اخضر اللون تحبه الاعراب وتتيبن به ويشهبون [al-qāriya ka-sāriya ṭāyir qaṣīr al-rijlayn ṭawīl al-minqār akhḍar al-lawn tuḥibbuhu al-aʿrāb wa-tatayabbanu bihi wa-yushahbūn] [col. 82] به الرجل السخي [bihi al-rajul al-sakhī] Karia, a noun of the same form as saria (that is, beam, Luc. VI, 41.), is a bird which has short feet, a long beak, a green colour (another copy has اخضر الظهر [akhḍar al-ẓahr] a green back); the Arabs love it, since they hold it a bird of good omen, and they compare a generous man to it. And Giauhari: القارية طير خضر تحبها الاعراب ويشهبون بها الرجل السخي وذلك لانها تنذر بالمطر [al-qāriya ṭayr khuḍr tuḥibbuhā al-aʿrāb wa-yushahbūn bihā al-rajul al-sakhī wa-dhālika li-annahā tundhiru bi-l-maṭar] Karia, a green bird, which the Arabs love and to which they compare a generous man, because it signals rain. And Alcamus: القارية طاير اذا راوه استبشروا بالمطر كانه رسول الغيث او مقدمة السحاب [al-qāriya ṭāyir idhā raʾawhu istabsharū bi-l-maṭar ka-annahu rasūl al-ghayth aw muqaddimat al-saḥāb] Karia, a bird at the sight of which people rejoice because of rain to come, as though it were the herald of the shower and the forerunner of the clouds. Again Damir, under the heading On its use: الحل لان العرب كانت تاكلها [al-ḥill li-anna al-ʿarab kānat taʾkuluhā] Eating it is permitted, because the Arabs eat it. And the book entitled الحج [al-ḥajj] Alchag, or Pilgrimage: الحمام يغدي بشاه وما دونه من القواري وغيرها يغدي بالقيمة [al-ḥamām yughdī bi-shāh wa-mā dūnahu min al-qawārī wa-ghayrihā yughdī bi-l-qīma] A dove (which one of the pilgrims has vowed to give as an offering at the tomb of the false prophet) is redeemed with a sheep; but whatever is below a dove (for example karia birds, or others like them) is redeemed by paying its price. From this Damir inferred two things: first, that the bird is edible; second, that it differs from the dove. However, Ibno Sachith, in the book On the Purity of Speech, defines القواري [al-qawārī], that is, karia birds, as طير خضر لها ترجيع [ṭayr khuḍr lahā tarjīʿ] green birds which make their voice reverberate in the throat, like a cooing dove, which is otherwise peculiar to those birds that drink water in a single draught. This is called عب [ʿabb] abba in Arabic.

These things having been thus explained, it follows that the bird קרא kore, or قارية [qāriya] karia if you prefer, as it is called in Arabic, is unknown to us, since it is clear that among us there is no [II, 635] bird to which all these marks apply. Yet of all the birds we know, the closest to it is Aristotle's ὁ σκολόπαξ [ho skolopax], or ἀσκολόπαξ [askolopax]. Gaza calls it gallinago; Pliny and Martial call it woodcock (rusticula) and rustica perdix [rustic partridge]; Nemesianus scolopax; the old Glosses acceia, whence the Tuscans to this day say acceiga; the Germans sneppa; and the French beccassa, from the size of its beak. To the same bird I refer the Hebrew קורא kore. For it is not formed from crying out, as people think, but from the noun קורה kora, which first means beam and timber, and then also a sharpened stake, from which fences are made. Hence the verb קרה kera, derived from it, means not only to lay beams and to floor with planks, as passim in Nehemiah, but also to fence in, or to repair a fence, as in the Talmudic tractate Moed Katon, ch. 1, fol. 7b: ומקרין את הפריצה במועד כיצד מקרין רב יוסף אמר בהוצא ודפני, One may also repair a breach in a fence on a festival day. But how is it repaired? Rabbi Joseph said: with stakes of palm and laurel. Thus, just as the σκολόπαξ [skolopax] is so called in Greek because it has a long, straight beak like a σκόλοψ [skolops], that is, a stake, so in Hebrew it is called קורא kore, because for the Hebrews קורה kora is not only δόκος [dokos] but also σκόλοψ [skolops]. So the reasoning is parallel. The final Aleph stands for He, as in נקרא 2 Sam. I, 6., and in the noun קראה [col. 83] for meeting, which comes from the verb קרה, to meet. Besides the size of the beak, the bird kore has this in common with the scolopax: both have short feet, both are edible, both live in the mountains. For just as David says that τὸν [ton] kore is hunted over the mountains, so Belon writes that the scolopax spends the summer in the Alps and the Pyrenees, and in the highest mountains of Switzerland, Savoy and Auvergne. Neither exceeds the bulk of a dove. For just as the قارية [qāriya] karia is defined by the Arabs as دون الحمام [dūn al-ḥamām] below a dove, so Nemesianus says of the scolopax:
— — the lovely scolopax is an easy prey: you will see it no larger in body than the Paphian birds.
